hints: At the maximum point $M$, the derivative of $y=\sin x\cos2x$ is zero.
Differentiate with the product rule to get $\cos x\cos2x-2\sin x\sin2x$.
Use double-angle identities to reduce the stationary-point equation, then select the root corresponding to the displayed maximum in the first positive section of the curve.
Evaluate that $x$-coordinate in radians and round only at the end to two decimal places.
walkthrough:
Differentiate $y = \sin x\cos 2x$ with respect to $x$ using the product rule:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = (\cos x)\cos 2x + (\sin x)(-2\sin 2x) = \cos x\cos 2x - 2\sin x\sin 2x$$

Use double-angle identities $\cos 2x = 1 - 2\sin^2 x$ and $\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x$:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \cos x(1 - 2\sin^2 x) - 2\sin x(2\sin x\cos x)$$
$$= \cos x(1 - 2\sin^2 x - 4\sin^2 x) = \cos x(1 - 6\sin^2 x)$$

Set $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 0$ for the maximum point $M$ in the first section of the curve where $\cos x > 0$:
$$1 - 6\sin^2 x = 0 \implies \sin^2 x = \dfrac{1}{6} \implies \sin x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}$$

ai_rubric.Finding Stationary Points: Applies the product rule, reaching a form such as $p\cos x\cos2x+q\sin x\sin2x$, or demonstrates full product-rule working; Derives $\frac{dy}{dx}=\cos x\cos2x-2\sin x\sin2x$, or equivalent; Concludes with $a=0.42$.

skill_tags: Finding an Area Under a Curve

hints: The curve lies below the $x$-axis across $R$, so its area is the negative of the corresponding definite integral.
From $\sin x\cos2x=0$ and the diagram, use the limits $x=\tfrac\pi4$ and $x=\tfrac{3\pi}4$.
Rewrite $\cos2x$ as $2\cos^2x-1$, and use $u=\cos x$ with $du=-\sin x\,dx$ to integrate exactly.
Evaluate at the exact limits and simplify the positive result using $\cos(\pi/4)=\sqrt2/2$ and $\cos(3\pi/4)=-\sqrt2/2$.
walkthrough:
Determine the limits for the shaded region $R$ below the $x$-axis from $\sin x\cos 2x = 0$:
In the interval $0 \leqslant x \leqslant \pi$, the curve crosses the axis at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

Express the integrand using $\cos 2x = 2\cos^2 x - 1$:
$$\sin x\cos 2x = \sin x(2\cos^2 x - 1) = 2\cos^2 x\sin x - \sin x$$

Integrate using the substitution $u = \cos x$ where $\mathrm{d}u = -\sin x\,\mathrm{d}x$:
$$\int (2\cos^2 x\sin x - \sin x)\,\mathrm{d}x = -\dfrac{2}{3}\cos^3 x + \cos x$$

Evaluate at the upper limit $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ where $\cos(3\pi/4) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$:
$$\left[-\dfrac{2}{3}\cos^3 x + \cos x\right]_{x=\frac{3\pi}{4}} = -\dfrac{2}{3}\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\right) - \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{6} - \dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{6} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{3}$$

Evaluate at the lower limit $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ where $\cos(\pi/4) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$:
$$\left[-\dfrac{2}{3}\cos^3 x + \cos x\right]_{x=\frac{\pi}{4}} = -\dfrac{2}{3}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\right) + \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{6} + \dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{6} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{3}$$

Calculate the area of region $R$ by taking the negative of the integral because $y \leqslant 0$ on this interval:
$$\text{Area} = -\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{3} - \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\right) = -\left(-\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}\right) = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}$$

ai_rubric.Finding an Area Under a Curve: Applies a double-angle formula and derives an integrand of the form $p\cos^3x+q\cos x$. Derives an antiderivative equivalent to $-\frac23\cos^3x+\cos x$, with sign for the displayed integral. The final result is $\dfrac{2\sqrt2}{3}$.
